## Causality

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
-   "How do we know if X **causes** y?"

-   Are our estimates **causal**? Academics fight about this all day!

-   This question is at center of **causal inference**

-   We will learn why it is so difficult to establish causality with data

-   We will also learn potential solutions
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![Pictured: audience at a research presentation](img/the-thing.png){fig-align='center' width=100%}
:::
:::


:::
:::::

## What do we mean by causality?

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
In this class, we say **X causes Y** if...

An **intervention** that changes the value of X produces a **probabilistic** change in Y

-   [Intervention]{.blue} = X is being **changed** or altered

-   [Probabilistic]{.red} = Y should change, *on average*, but need not in every instance
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](img/hume.jpeg){fig-align='center' width=70%}
:::
:::


:::
:::::

## Interventions and probability

How do the two parts of our definition fit here?

> Aspirin causes a reduction in fever symptoms

. . .

[Intervention]{.blue} = someone **takes** aspirin, we administer aspirin, we sneak it into someone's food, etc.

. . .

[Outcome]{.red} = Taking aspirin doesn't work 100% of the time; but *in general*, *on average*, *more often than not*, etc., taking aspirin $\rightarrow$ less fever

. . .

What about this example? Democratic institutions reduce the incidence of interstate war

## \# The problem with causality {.center background-color="#dc354a"}

## Not obvious: education and earnings

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
-   Positive correlation between education and earnings, yet
-   People who are already wealthy (or likely to become wealthy) get more education than people who are not wealthy
-   In other words: people **self-select** into education levels
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](img/education.png){fig-align='center' width=100%}
:::
:::


:::
:::::


## The trouble with causality

. . .

We can't directly observe a change in X **causing** a change in Y

. . .

This is true even in **experiments**, where we directly manipulate stuff

. . .

All we can see are **correlations** between X and Y

. . .

Some of those correlations **are** causal; some **are not**; how can we tell?

# Where does it all go wrong then? {.center background-color="#dc354a"}

## The Democratic Peace?

Does the spread of democracy reduce international conflict?

. . .

Theory: war is costly and the costs are borne by citizens; countries where citizens have more input $\rightarrow$ less conflict

. . .

X here is [whether the country is a democracy]{.blue} (versus autocracy)

Y is [the number of wars the country is involved in]{.red}

. . .

Ideal, imaginary approach: take a country, look at Y when democracy = 1, and then when democracy = 0

. . .

Do this for all countries, take the average

## Potential outcomes

This magical world where we can compare the number of wars when a country is a democracy versus when it is not is called the **potential outcomes**



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}


|country | democracy| war|
|:-------|---------:|---:|
|Canada  |         0|   2|
|Canada  |         1|   3|
|China   |         0|   6|
|China   |         1|   2|
|USA     |         0|   5|
|USA     |         1|   2|


:::
:::



## Potential vs. observed

We only **observe** the world on the right, but not the left

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}


Table: Potential outcomes world

|country | democracy| war|
|:-------|---------:|---:|
|Canada  |         0|   2|
|Canada  |         1|   3|
|China   |         0|   6|
|China   |         1|   2|
|USA     |         0|   5|
|USA     |         1|   2|


:::
:::


:::

::: {.column width="50%"}


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}


Table: Observed outcomes world

|country | democracy| war|
|:-------|---------:|---:|
|Canada  |         0|  NA|
|Canada  |         1|   3|
|China   |         0|   6|
|China   |         1|  NA|
|USA     |         0|  NA|
|USA     |         1|   2|


:::
:::


:::
:::::

## The fundamental problem of causality

. . .

We have missing data on "what would have happened" had the US been an autocracy

. . .

"what would have happened" $\rightarrow$ the **counterfactual**

. . .

Our goal in causal inference is to make as good a guess as possible as to what Y would have been had democracy = 0 instead of 1 (and vice versa)

## Comparing apples and oranges

Implicitly, this means we are saying the countries that are *autocracies* are good **counterfactuals** for the countries that are democracies (and vice versa)

. . .

For instance, that China is a good counterfactual for the US

. . .

But China and the US are different in so many ways! They are not good **counterfactuals** of one another

. . .

We will see *exactly why* this is a problem in the following weeks


## Example: ideology

Where does (liberal) ideology come from?

. . .

Variables in the literature: Income (I), Liberal (L), Age (A), Media (M), Parents (P)

. . .



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](lec-6_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-7-1.png){fig-align='center' width=70%}
:::
:::



::: notes
What are our assumptions? What's this diagram saying (FYI its called a DAG)?
:::

## Waffles and Divorce



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](img/waffle-house.png){fig-align='center' width=100%}
:::
:::



## Does Waffle House cause divorce?

Do cheap, delicious waffles put marriages at risk?



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](lec-6_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-9-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%}
:::
:::



::: notes
Speculate on underlying mechanism
:::

## Does Waffle House cause divorce?

. . .

Almost certainly *not*

. . .

No one thinks there is a *plausible* way in which Waffle House causes divorce

. . .

When we see a correlation of this kind we wonder about other variables that are **actually** driving the relationship

. . .

You've likely thought about this before: *a "lurking" variable, "other factors", that "matter"*

. . .

But what might that *variable* be? And *how* exactly does it lead us astray?

## The lurking variable

It turns out that Waffle Houses originated in the South (Georgia), and most of them are still there

. . .

The South also happens to have some of the highest divorce rates in the country

## What about location?

A lurking variable in this case could be the south! So for example, South **has an effect on** Waffle Houses and Divorce, but Waffles **do not cause** Divorce



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](lec-6_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png){fig-align='center' width=80%}
:::
:::



. . .

This is called **confounding**: the South is **confounding** the relationship between Waffles and Divorce

## A totally confounded relationship

The a confounded relationship like the one on the left will produce an association like the one on the right

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](lec-6_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-11-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%}
:::
:::


:::

::: {.column width="50%"}


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](lec-6_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-12-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%}
:::
:::


:::
:::::

Even if Waffles and Divorce are **causally** unrelated

## What's going on here?

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
Think of causality as water flowing in the direction of the arrows

We want look at water flowing **directly** from a **treatment** to an **outcome**

But **account** for the fact that there is often *indirect* flow that *contaminates* our estimates
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}


{{< video "img/confound-heiss.mp4" >}}




Source: the mighty Andrew Heiss
:::
:::::

## What's going on here?

To **identify** the effect of Waffles on Divorce we need to **account**, or **control for**, the influence of the South

Otherwise we will be *confounded*



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](lec-6_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-13-1.png){fig-align='center' width=80%}
:::
:::



## The confounding fork 🍴

Y $\leftarrow$ Z $\rightarrow$ X

There is a third variable, Z, that is a **common cause** of X and Y



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](lec-6_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-14-1.png){fig-align='center' width=90%}
:::
:::



## The confounding fork

We've already seen this!

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](lec-6_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-15-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%}
:::
:::



Creates an association between X and Y that isn't causal
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](lec-6_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-16-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%}
:::
:::



Distorts the true causal relation between X and Y
:::
:::::

Note that **both** of these fork scenarios will **confound**

## Dealing with forks

We need to figure out what Z is, measure it, and **adjust for it** in our analysis



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](lec-6_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-17-1.png){fig-align='center' width=90%}
:::
:::



# The pipe 🚰 {.center background-color="#dc354a"}

## The perplexing pipe 🚰

X $\rightarrow$ Z $\rightarrow$ Y

X causes Z, which causes Y (or: Z *mediates* the effect of X on Y)

. . .



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](lec-6_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-18-1.png){fig-align='center' width=50%}
:::
:::



What happens if we **adjust for Z**? We **block** the effect of X on Y

## An example: foreign intervention

What effect does [US foreign wars]{.blue} have on [US support abroad]{.red}?

. . .

Say the DAG looks like this:



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](lec-6_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-19-1.png){fig-align='center' width=50%}
:::
:::



If we control for *casualties* we are *blocking* the effect of intervention on support

## An example: foreign intervention

What if the relationship instead looked like this:



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](lec-6_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-20-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%}
:::
:::



::: notes
What does it mean
:::

## An example: foreign intervention

Two ways that War affects US sentiment: directly and indirectly

Adjusting for **casualties** blocks the *indirect* effect; if that's what we want, fine -- But if we want the full effect then we'll be wrong!



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](lec-6_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-21-1.png){fig-align='center' width=80%}
:::
:::



::: notes
What does it mean
:::

## Pipes: why are they even a problem?

Just leave pipes alone! It's a problem of "over-adjusting"

. . .

Bad social science: sometimes we are so afraid of **forks** that we control for everything we have data on

. . .

Especially when a process seems very complicated

## Example: where pipes go wrong

The effects of **smoking** on **heart problems** might be complex; lots of potential confounds to worry about

. . .

Researcher might think they need to control for a study subject's **cholesterol** because cholesterol affects heart health

. . .

"We should compare people who smoke but have similar levels of cholesterol, because cholesterol affects heart health"

## Example: where pipes go wrong

If the DAG looks like this, **cholesterol** is a pipe and controlling is bad!

. . .



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](lec-6_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-22-1.png){fig-align='center' width=80%}
:::
:::



# The collider 💥 {.center background-color="#dc354a"}

## The explosive collider 💥

$X \rightarrow Z \leftarrow Y$

. . .

X and Y have a common **effect**

. . .

Left alone, it's no problem; but **controlling for Z** creates strange patterns

. . .



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](lec-6_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-23-1.png){fig-align='center' width=60%}
:::
:::



## Example: the NBA



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](img/nba-height.png){fig-align='center' width=50%}
:::
:::



. . .

Should the NBA stop worrying about height when drafting players?

## No!

Obviously, height helps in basketball

. . .

But **among NBA players** there might be no relationship between height and scoring, because...

. . .

The shorter players **who are drafted** have other advantages

. . .

**Among NBA players** = adjusting, or controlling for, being in the NBA

. . .



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](lec-6_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-25-1.png){fig-align='center' width=50%}
:::
:::



## Another example: bad findings

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
Richard McElreath asks: why are surprising findings so often untrustworthy?
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](img/hurricanes.png){fig-align='center' width=100%}
:::
:::


:::
:::::

## Another example: bad findings



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](img/shark-elections.png){fig-align='center' width=60%}
:::
:::



## It's a collider

Imagine that in reality there is no relationship between how **surprising** a finding is and how **trustworthy** it is



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](lec-6_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-28-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%}
:::
:::



## It's a collider

But now imagine that studies are only published **either** if they're *very trustworthy* OR *very surprising*



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](lec-6_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-29-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%}
:::
:::



## It's a collider

By only looking at *published papers* (e.g., **controlling for publication**), we create a negative relationship that doesn't exist



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](lec-6_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-30-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%}
:::
:::



## Exploding colliders

Like pipes, colliders are a problem of controlling for the wrong thing

They are often the result of a **sample selection** problem

They can **obscure** actual relationships or **fabricate** non-existent ones

We need to avoid controlling for colliders; but they are everywhere!

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](lec-6_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-31-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%}
:::
:::


:::

::: {.column width="50%"}


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](lec-6_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-32-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%}
:::
:::


:::
:::::

## 💥 Your turn: colliders 💥

How are the following examples of colliders?

1.  Among employees at Google, there is a strong negative correlation between technical skills and social skills.

2.  A study of people who tested for COVID finds that people who smoke regularly are *less likely* to develop COVID-19. A real study!

::: notes
we are conditioning on testing, these are the only people we observe anything that's correlated with likelihood of testing here becomes a problem who gets tested? imagine that healthcare workers get tested a lot, and that people who actually have COVID 19 are tested a lot so smokers with no symptoms are very unlikely to be in the data so of those tested, non-smokers are more likely to have COVID19 than smokers
:::

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
